transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

Um… yeah, I came in because I’m having this thing where, mostly at night when I’m by myself, I start eating and then it’s like I can’t stop. Like I’ll be standing there telling myself, “Okay, put it away, that’s enough,” but it feels like something else takes over.

It’s weird because during the day I can be pretty normal, I’m at work with the animals and there’s a routine and all that—actually routines help a lot with animals, you know, they get stressed if things change—but then at home it’s like the routine just disappears. And I end up eating way more than I meant to, even while I’m aware I should stop. It’s embarrassing to say out loud.
After these nighttime eating episodes, do you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or do anything else to try to prevent gaining weight?

Yeah… I do. I mean, not laxatives, really, but after I eat like that I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up. It’s like my brain says I have to undo it before it… I don’t know, before the calories settle in or something.

I know that probably sounds irrational. I work with animals, and if one of them eats something they shouldn’t, we’re very careful and calm about it, but with me I just panic. It feels like the only way to fix what I just did.
Do these nighttime eating episodes and the things you do afterward, like making yourself vomit, cause you a lot of distress or interfere with your daily life?

Yeah, it does. I mean… I keep trying to tell myself it’s contained, like it’s just at night, but then it sort of leaks into the next day.

Like at work, I had this bilingual outreach presentation—well, “bilingual” sounds fancier than it was, it was just for community visitors, and I always worry I’m going to mess up the Spanish parts even though I practiced—and the whole time I kept thinking about leaving afterward. Not even the presentation, really. Just getting out of there.

And because of that I stumbled through parts of it, lost my place, and afterward I was just standing there thinking, great, everyone noticed. My coworkers probably saw I wasn’t fully there. So… yeah, it’s not just embarrassing at home. It’s starting to mess with my work, too.
Can you describe what goes through your mind right before these nighttime eating episodes start? Do you feel like you have no control over your eating once it begins?

Right before it starts, it’s usually like… I’m alone and my mind is kind of buzzing. I’ll think, “I’ll just have a little bit,” or “I’m just going to check what’s in the kitchen,” which sounds ridiculous when I say it because I know where everything is.

And then once I start eating, yeah, it really does feel like I don’t have control. I’ll be telling myself, “Stop, put it away, you don’t need more,” and at the same time I’m still reaching for more. It’s like something takes over.

It reminds me of when one of the animals gets fixated on something and you can’t redirect them easily—sorry, that’s probably not the point. But that’s how it feels. I’m there, I know what I should do, but I can’t seem to make myself stop.
During these nighttime eating episodes, would you say that you feel a complete lack of control over your eating, like you can’t stop once you start?

Yeah… that’s honestly why I came in. Once I start eating alone at night, it feels like something kind of takes over, and I can’t stop.

I’ll be standing there telling myself, “Put it away, just close the cabinet,” and then I’m still eating. It’s weird because at work I can follow routines really carefully—feeding schedules, cleaning protocols, all of that—but with this, in the moment, it’s like that part of my brain doesn’t listen. So yes, it feels like a loss of control.
Are you fully awake and aware during these nighttime eating episodes, or do you feel like you're in a daze or not completely in control of your actions?

I’m awake, yeah. I don’t think it’s like sleepwalking or anything like that. I know what I’m doing, which is part of what makes it feel so awful.

It’s more that once I’m alone at night and I start eating, it’s like something takes over. I’ll be thinking, very clearly, “Put it away, stop, close the cabinet,” and then my hand is still going back for more. Like I’m aware, but I’m not really able to steer it, if that makes sense.

Sorry, I know that’s not exactly… I just mean I’m not in a fog. I’m there. I just can’t seem to stop once it starts.
How often do you make yourself vomit after these nighttime eating episodes—do you do this nearly every time, or only occasionally?

Usually… yeah. I mean, not like I sit there and plan it exactly, but after I eat like that I almost always end up in the bathroom making myself throw up.

It feels like the only way to undo what I just did, like before the calories really… settle in, I guess. Which I know sounds messed up. Sometimes I’ll tell myself I won’t do it this time, and then I’m already in there.

Sorry, I know you asked how often. It’s… most of the time after those episodes.
Do you make yourself vomit or do anything else to compensate for the food you eat during these nighttime episodes?

Yeah… I mean, mostly I make myself throw up after. That’s the main thing.

After I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom, and it feels like I have to get it out before the calories sort of… settle in or count, I guess. I know that probably doesn’t make sense. It’s like when I’m cleaning cages at work, if something spills you just fix it right away before it spreads—sorry, that’s not really the same thing.

But yes, I do make myself vomit after those episodes. Usually.
Besides making yourself vomit, do you ever fast, exercise excessively, or do anything else to make up for the food you eat during these nighttime episodes?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that. The throwing up is the thing I know I do. The rest… I don’t know if I’d call it “making up for it,” exactly.

Like, some days I might eat less afterward because I feel guilty or gross, but I’m not sure if that counts as fasting. And exercise—my job is already pretty physical, with lifting bags of feed and cleaning enclosures and all that, so sometimes I tell myself I’ve “worked it off,” but that’s not really like going to a gym for hours or anything.

Sorry, I’m kind of circling around it. I guess I don’t have a clear answer beyond the vomiting.
Do you ever go without eating for the rest of the day or push yourself to exercise more than usual after these nighttime eating episodes?

I… don’t really know if I’d say that. Like, sometimes the next day I’m not hungry, or I feel kind of off and I’ll just sort of skip around meals, but I don’t sit there with a plan like, “Okay, no food for the rest of the day.” At least I don’t think of it that way.

And with exercise, not really in a formal sense. I mean, work can be a lot—hauling stuff, cleaning, walking back and forth all day—so sometimes my brain turns that into, like, “Well, that probably helped,” but I’m not going out for extra runs or anything after it.

Sorry, I’m probably making that more complicated than it needs to be. I guess I’m not totally sure.
Do you ever go for extended periods without eating or push yourself to do more physical activity than usual after these nighttime eating episodes to try to balance out what you ate?

I’m not sure I can say that clearly. I don’t think I’m, like, deliberately setting out to not eat for a long time, if that’s what you mean. Sometimes I’ll avoid food for a while because I feel bad about what happened, but then other times I just get busy at work and miss eating because there’s a sick animal or something needs cleaning, and then it all kind of blends together.

With the physical activity… I don’t really go out of my way to do extra exercise, I don’t think. My job is already a lot of moving around, and sometimes I sort of tell myself that counts, but I’m not making a whole plan to “balance it out,” I guess.

Sorry, I know that’s not a very direct answer. I just don’t really track it that way.
Do you ever intentionally go for long periods without eating or push yourself to do a lot more physical activity than usual after these nighttime eating episodes to try to make up for what you ate?

I don’t think I can give you a clean yes or no. I don’t, like, decide “I’m not eating today” to cancel it out, if that’s what you mean. Sometimes I’ll just put off eating because I feel weird about it, but then I’ll get distracted—work gets chaotic, and there’s always something with the animals, like someone didn’t latch a gate right or a kennel needs scrubbing—so I don’t always know what’s intentional and what’s just the day getting away from me.

And the activity thing… I’m already on my feet a lot, so I don’t usually add extra exercise on top of that. I might think, “Well, at least I was moving all day,” but I’m not sure that’s the same as trying to make up for it. So… I guess I’m not really sure.

Do you ever have episodes where you eat a large amount of food in a short period of time, even when you’re not hungry, and feel like you can’t stop yourself, but you don’t make yourself vomit or do anything else afterward?

Yeah… that’s kind of the main thing, honestly. Like, the reason I came in is because once I start eating at night—usually when I’m by myself—it feels like something just takes over. I’ll be telling myself, “Okay, put it away, that’s enough,” and then I’m still standing there eating.

It’s not even always because I’m hungry. Sometimes I’m just tired or wired from the day, and then it’s like I lose the thread completely. Sorry, I’m thinking of when I get home from work and the house is quiet, which sounds nice, but it’s also when I kind of… I don’t know, get stuck in that pattern. So yes, the not-being-able-to-stop part is definitely there.
Can you describe exactly what it feels like during those nighttime eating episodes—specifically, do you feel like you're not in control of your actions even though you're fully awake and aware?

Yeah… I mean, I’m awake. I know what I’m doing. It’s not like I black out or anything. But it feels like once I start eating alone at night, something kind of takes over.

I’ll be standing there telling myself, “Put it away, stop, go to bed,” and then I’m still reaching for more. It’s weird because part of me is very aware of it, like I can hear myself thinking that I should stop, but my body just keeps doing it. Like when I’m at work and one of the animals gets fixated on a thing and you can’t redirect them easily—sorry, that’s probably a weird comparison—but that’s sort of how it feels.

So yes, I guess I do feel not in control, even though I’m fully awake and know it’s happening.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a sense of loss of control during the nighttime eating episodes, which is key to differentiating between the remaining candidates.
doctor.question: Can you describe exactly what it feels like during those nighttime eating episodes—specifically, do you feel like you're not in control of your actions even though you're fully awake and aware?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: I came in because once I start eating alone at night, it feels like something takes over and I can't stop, even while I'm telling myself to put the food away.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during nighttime eating episodes, I feel unable to control my actions despite being awake and aware, which directly matches loss of control over eating.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I’m awake. I know what I’m doing. It’s not like I black out or anything. But it feels like once I start eating alone at night, something kind of takes over.

I’ll be standing there telling myself, “Put it away, stop, go to bed,” and then I’m still reaching for more. It’s weird because part of me is very aware of it, like I can hear myself thinking that I should stop, but my body just keeps doing it. Like when I’m at work and one of the animals gets fixated on a thing and you can’t redirect them easily—sorry, that’s probably a weird comparison—but that’s sort of how it feels.

So yes, I guess I do feel not in control, even though I’m fully awake and know it’s happening.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent episodes of binge eating accompanied by a sense of loss of control during these episodes and recurrent compensatory behaviors (self-induced vomiting) to prevent weight gain. There is no evidence of regular use of other compensatory mechanisms such as laxatives, fasting, or excessive exercise, which supports the diagnosis of Other Specified Eating or Feeding Disorder (OSFED), specifically atypical anorexia nervosa or subthreshold bulimia nervosa. The absence of strictly defined episodic loss of control eating disorder criteria (e.g., frequency) supports F50.81 over F50.2 (Bulimia nervosa).
